title: The man born blind. Part 2
scripture_text: ‘’As he went along, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” “Neither this man nor his parents sinned,”said Jesus, “but this happened so that the works of God might be displayed in him. As long as it is day, we must do the works of him who sent me. Night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” After saying this, he spit on the ground, made some mud with the saliva, and put it on the man’s eyes. “Go,” he told him, “wash in the Pool of Siloam” (this word means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came home seeing.’’
devotional:
The questions the disciples asked.

‘’Rabbi, who has sinned this man or his parents that he was born blind?’’

How different is the perspective of the disciples to that of Jesus? If you read what John says carefully you will notice that it was Jesus who saw the blind man ‘As he went along, he saw a blind man.’ It was Jesus’ noticing the blind man that drew his disciple’s attention to him. They see the blind beggar as a case study, a topic for theological discussion and debate.

Often when we are faced with situations when we don’t know what to do, so we begin to hide our impotence with words and discussions, often meaningless! The question they asked was none of their business. They didn’t discuss how they could help the man, or what practical support they could give him. There is a clue in their question that explains their inability to offer any practical help. They defined this man in terms of his supposed sin. They looked upon him as a sinner, justifying their inability to offer him practical help.

What can we learn from their question?

The theological problem in Judaism was to explain the cause of birth defects. The question of whether a disabled child suffered the disability from the sins of their parents or his/her own pre-natal sin was actively debated in Judaism. There was actually a rabbinic pronouncement from near the time of Jesus, "When a pregnant woman worships in a heathen temple the fetus also commits idolatry." Therefore, when a baby was born who was anything less than perfect, blame could be placed on the child if no sin were evident in the parents.

In the first century the popular folk-lore of the Jews saw a direct connection between illness and sin. They lived in a cause and effect world. Bad things happen to bad people. Good things happen to good people. In a cause and effect world, everything is orderly, predictable, and understandable. In a "cause and effect" world, those who study the hardest, excel; those who work the longest, prosper. There are a number of things we need to notice about this faulty theology.

It is worth noting that there can be a connection between sin and suffering. This was not true in the case of this blind man, but it can be true. Not all suffering is caused by sin, but sin does cause suffering. Jesus shows us that sin and suffering are not always related, but not that they are never related. There are texts in Scripture that clearly indicate that people are hurting and suffering and physically depraved and deprived because of their own evil ways. See 1 Corinthians 11:30.

We are not in a position to decide or judge if a person is suffering because of sin, that is for God to know, not us; that kind of knowledge would be too dangerous for us to have. The cause of suffering should not determine our response to it.

Do children suffer because of their parent’s sin?

The Old Testament teaches ‘You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the waters below. You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the lord your God, am a jealous God, punishing the children for the sins of their fathers to the third and forth generations of those who hate me.’ Exodus 20:4-5.

These verses are speaking in a general sense, not specific. He is not saying when daddy sins junior gets it. He is saying when the fathers, plural, sin, the generations, plural, pay. What does this mean? When Israel goes into idolatry and God punishes Israel by oppression, by scattering them, it's not only that generation that gets punished but it's the rest of the generations that follow. He is talking about national punishment. It’s not talking about particular sin of the father and the son gets punished. God doesn't operate like that but Israel thought He did.

The Old Testament says ‘The soul who sins is the one who will die. The son will not share the guilt of the father, nor will the father share the guilt of son. The righteousness of the righteous man will be credited to him, and the wickedness of the wicked will be charged against him.’ Ezekiel 18:20.

So the question that the disciples asked was somewhat redundant. Would an answer to the question help them minister to the blind man? Would they have been better equipped to meet the man’s needs if they had known if he or his parents had been the cause of his suffering?

There is something within all of us that wants to understand and explain suffering. We think that if we had some answers we would cope better, we fear the mystery that suffering brings.

In the preface of his book The Problem of Pain, C.S. Lewis wrote:

‘For the far higher task of teaching fortitude and patience I was never fool enough to suppose myself qualified, nor have I anything to offer my readers except my conviction that when pain is to be borne, a little courage helps more than much knowledge, a little human sympathy more than much courage, and the least tincture of the love of God more than all.”
prayer: Father sometimes theological debate robs us of the ability to show practical care for others.
